The Epic African Electrical Motorcycle Road Trip

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight we let the sun power us across Africa on a rugged motorbike with a team of scientists...proving it can be done

Unique Selling Point:
We will tell a story of a group of students and academics who proved that the African sun can power a locally-made motorbike across four countries from Nairobi to Stellenbosch in two and a half weeks, despite there being no charging stations on the route. While being a scientific experiment, it was also a stunt to raise awareness about the potential for Electric Vehicles in Africa, while championing local skills, both the expertise of the students from the US and in the ROAM motorbike factory in Kenya.


Summary:
The story will be told through interviews with the four people below, a bit of B-Roll filmed in their interviews, and through a daily video diary the team kept as they travelled 17 days from Nairobi and Stellenbosch, arriving here on the 16th of October.

It was the brainchild of PROF THINUS BOOYSEN, founder of the University of Stellenbosch’s Electric Mobility Lab, who is pushing research in affordable electric vehicles that are rugged enough for the African continent, for working people, and made on the continent.

The motorbikes were mostly driven by Stellenbosch Doctoral Student STEPHAN LACOCK and Kenyan engineer MASALULE KITUYI of ROAM, the Swedish-Kenyan company that makes these tough, rugged Electrical motorbikes. In Kenya, they are used a lot as delivery bikes. Tther members of the team, which included Stephan’s father and brother, and THINUS BOOYSEN, also drove the bike as part of the team experience.

We also interview DR JASON SAMUELS who works in a private company GREENX across the road from the Department of Electrical Engineering, and was in charge of the solar panel element of the trip. His company puts up solar panels on schools across the country, sponsored by the University of Stellenbosch. His dream is to use this research to build a model where schools can power their electric buses with the solar power on the roofs to provide transport locally for school kids. When we do the interview, he will take us to a school and show us what he does. It will provide us with a different but clear application of renewable energy visually.

The three South African interviews are confirmed, but I am still waiting to hear if we can interview MASA KITUYI by zoom as he is back in Nairobi. MASA KITUYI is the lead engineer on the ROAM motorbike product, and a motorbike stunt driver.

The team of four people drove up from Stellenbosch to Nairobi in mid-September with a custom built bakkie, holding solar panels and a large battery. Once they got to Nairobi, they had to haggle ROAM for enough smaller motorbike batteries to make the trip possible. They managed to persuade them to increase an initial offer of four to ten. ROAM lent them two bikes, one of which was in the back of the bakkie as a back-up should the first fail. The riders swapped out but mostly Stephan Lacock and Masa Kituyi rode the bikes.

They then set out and drove 6000km through Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia and Botswana to South Africa, experiencing sun, clouds, rain and hail, traffic and empty landscapes. They camped most nights where they stopped, on the side of the road.

They travelled as two teams over 17 days. Every morning the solar panel team would set off at about 4:00 am, drive 200km to find a good sunny spot to put down the solar panels – a soccer field, or a river bed, or just by the side of the road. This team would charge the huge battery they had bought from South Africa while waiting for the motor-biker to arrive. At first light, the motorbike would set out with a support car, swapping out the small electric battery every 50 to 100kms, depending on weather and traffic conditions. Once the biker had caught up with the solar panel team, they would do another set of battery swaps and swap the bike-rider out. All this time, the solar panels would be recharging the big mother battery which would also be used to power the bike batteries at night.

Then the biker would set out again and do another 200 kms about to find the place where they could camp for the night. And at about four, once the sun started losing its power and angles, the solar panel team would pack up and follow them, getting there at about 08h00 pm to set up camp for the night, and prepare for a 4 am start the next morning.

This above information would be best presented or supported by a graphic with a map to show their route.

The video diary is fairly shakily shot with moments captured here and there, rather than a cinematographic spread. But there are some splendid drone shots which are very useful and it is more cinema verité than National Geographic. They have 1.2 TBs which is usefully organised and labelled.

The students were collecting data on battery consumption and vehicle efficiency, which is to show how many units of energy they used per km to show that EV’s are viable over long-distance, even without charging stations.

They discovered that there were a number of factors which impacted on their progress:

They weight of the driver
The contour and steepness of the road
The weather, in particular the wind while driving
The weather, in particular when there was not sun enough to power the batteries through the solar panels
The traffic – driving behind big trucks protected them from the wind and saved energy
The temperature – the higher the better
The efficiency of the driving – the more acceleration, the harder on the battery
The speed they drove

While the quest was a scientific experiment, it also became a personal and emotional journey for the participants. They found that they could break down barriers between people and themselves by explaining the electric bike and interacting with people along the way. There are some good moments that are caught on camera of these interactions, but not beautifully shot.

Tension moments on the road were:
• When it rained in Malawi and their progress was slowed down due to lack of sun and camping space
• When it hailed – more of a surprise than anything else
• When they set up the solar panel field next to the Lusaka airport and police tried to chase them away (no visuals of police but visuals of their solar camp)
• When they moved away from the equator and the tilt of the earth required a greater tilt of the solar panels to capture the sun’s rays, and they battled to find the right things to prop them up on
• A decision to do a 1000km final day finish to show that the motorbike could do that distance in a single day – and then made it.

Script:


(VO1) HERE COMES THE SUN….
A SOURCE OF LIGHT…AND POWER….
IT WAS SUNSHINE THAT POWERED THIS ELECTRIC MOTORBIKE OVER SIX THOUSAND KILOMETRES…..
ON AN EPIC ROAD TRIP ACROSS AFRICA.

Stephan Lacock soundup: We only had 19 days…

Jason Samuels soundup: A lot was on the line…

Thinus Booysen soundup: We were really scared that it wasn't going to work…

Masa Kituyi soundup: Everyone thought that we were crazy when we started saying that we're going to do this trip.

ERIN BATES: THE ROAD-TRIP WAS A BOLD IDEA, HATCHED BY ENGINEERS FROM STELLENBOSCH UNIVERSITY WHICH IS PIONEERING RESEARCH ON ELECTRIC TRANSPORT IN AFRICA.

(VO2) INITIALLY THE PROJECT WAS AN ATTEMPT TO SOLVE A PROBLEM: HOW TO GET TWO BATTERY-POWERED ELECTRIC MOTOR-BIKES FROM NAIROBI IN KENYA TO THE CAMPUS, AS PART OF A RESEARCH PARTNERSHIP BETWEEN THE UNIVERSITY AND A COMPANY CALLED ROAM ELECTRIC.

Stephan Lacock Soundup: Dis gerreid op 200 kilogram…

AND IN THIS DIFFICULTY, PROFESSOR THINUS BOOYSEN OF THE ENGINEERING FACULTY SAW AN OPPORTUNITY.

Prof Thinus Booysen
Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University
The quotes for couriers were just too much, or they weren't willing to travel with the batteries….and we said, we have six weeks. Let's plan this. Let's go up into Africa, get the bikes, ride them down, and then make a spectacle out of it.

(VO3) THINUS UPPED THE ANTE BY INSISTING ON USING GREEN ENERGY ON A ROUTE THAT HAS NO ELECTRICAL CHARGING STATIONS.
SO HE AND HIS PHD STUDENT, STEPHAN LACOCK, STARTED TO IMAGINE HOW THIS MIGHT WORK USING A COMBINATION OF SOLAR PANELS AND BATTERIES.

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
We didn’t know if it was possible, but the more effort we put in the more I realised it’s actually possibly and we just kept on pushing.

Prof Thinus Booysen
Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University
I spent weekends doing and redoing the math, because it's actually quite complicated. You have to think about the dynamics of the vehicle that's carrying the solar panels, and the motorbike, and understand how many kilometres you can do in a day, because they can never go too far away from one another,

(VO4) THEY DESIGNED A TRAVELLING POP-UP SOLAR PANEL ARRAY, WHICH THEY BELIEVED COULD GET THE TWO-WHEELER ABOUT 400 KMS A DAY.

Sound-Up: Time is of the essence. It is a thing.

(VO5) TEN SOLAR PANELS AND A LARGE BATTERY BANK WERE FITTED INTO A CUSTOMISED BAKKIE WHICH THEY CALLED THE BOSKRAAI.

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
I mean, the amount of weight that was in the back of that bakkie was just unbelievable. It was anything close to 1.2 tons. A lot of engineers, a lot of opinions went into one wooden box, but I mean it helped it's durability and everything in structure.

Sound-Up: Now for the last final check!

(VO6) SOME OF THE TEAM DROVE UP TO NAIROBI.
OTHERS JETTED IN, INCLUDING A SOLAR EXPERT, ONE OF THINUS’S FORMER STUDENTS, DR JASON SAMUELS.
JASON’S JOB WAS TO CHASE THE SUN IN THE BOSKRAAI BAKKIE AND SET UP THE SOLAR PANELS TO HARVEST MAXIMUM POWER.

Dr Jason Samuels
CEO, GreenX Engineering
We'd have to find a perfect spot ….. somewhere where it's open, but we could still get some community interaction, somewhere we not have a lot of shading, and also somewhere we will where we would not be chased away.

(VO7) BUT FIRST, THE SOUTH AFRICANS MET A KEY MEMBER OF THE TEAM, KENYAN MASA KITUYI, A VETERAN MOTOR-CROSS RACER.
AS AN ENGINEER, MASA HAD PLAYED A KEY ROLE IN DEVELOPING THE BIKE THEY WERE TAKING TO STELLENBOSCH.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
For me, it was always on the bucket list. I've always wanted to drive, uh, ride a motorcycle across Africa, but it was a bit daunting to do it on a motorbike that you've developed and been building for quite a while.

(VO8) THE ROAM-AIR MOTORBIKE IS RUGGED AND POPULAR ON THE STREETS OF NAIROBI. - THE FACTORY PRODUCES 40 BIKES A DAY, AND IS POISED TO CAPITALISE ON THE GROWING DEMAND FOR ELECTRIC VEHICLES.

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
When you walk through the door, there's this massive warehouse, and it's just electric motorcycles everywhere.

(VO9) EACH BIKE CARRIES TWO BATTERIES WHICH CAN BE CHARGED FROM A DOMESTIC POWER PLUG AND SWAPPED OUT.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
The motor bikes are used as a workhorse by Boda Boda riders around town, and they ride 13 hours a day, every single day. We've designed it to carry up to 220 kilos of payload.

(VO10) NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME THE BIKE WAS GOING TO BE TESTED ON DISTANCE - A 6000 KM ROUTE WHICH TRAVERSED SIX AFRICAN COUNTRIES.
ON THE 29TH OF SEPTEMBER THE TEAM SET OFF, KNOWING THAT THEY HAD TO QUICKLY SET UP A BATTERY-POWERING AND SWAPPING ROUTINE.

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
Every morning, around 4:30am I woke up, along with the team, we looked at the weather apps, with four weather apps just checking: where's the sun going to shine?

(VO11) THE DRIVING TEAM SET OFF AN HOUR AFTER THE SOLAR TEAM, WITH A BACK UP VEHICLE BEHIND, OFTEN DRIVEN BY STEFAN’S FATHER, RYNO LACOCK. RYNO HAS SPENT DECADES MANAGING ESKOM POWER PLANTS - NOW HE WAS CHAPERONING THE NEXT GENERATION AND LETTING THEM TAKE THE LEAD.

Ryno Lacock
Electrical Engineer
I ended up being the old cliche, chief cook and bottle washer on the trip because I was facilitating the whole thing in terms of camping and the cooking and so on

Ryno Lacock Upsound: Alright Masa we have calculated our distance to the solar team and what they are receiving, so you have a green light. …You have done 87.2 kilometeres already, 87.2.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
It did feel very clean as we moved around, just harnessing the sun's energy, but it did add quite a lot of pressure onto the timeline.

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
The motorcycle really had to go through quite different environments in terms of altitude, plateaus, you know, temperature, rain, everything.

(VO12) PROGRESS HINGED ON A CLEAR SKY.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
We need to make sure that we have sunlight and that that did change the dynamic a lot. You can plan as much as you want, but Mother Nature has its own say in what to do.

Instagram: Stephan Lacock
We are here in a hail storm in the middle of Maka Bako in Tanzania, crazy to see the people’s reactions, our own as well, slipping a lot, but very cool and excited.

Masa Kituyi soundup: It’s been a crazy afternoon. I am happy I am still warm and dry!

(VO13) THE TEAM HAD TO WORK WITH THEIR OWN BODY WEIGHT FOR MAXIMUM EFFICIENCY.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
In Malawi, we were driving up 2000 meters above sea level, climb from the Lake Malawi up into the forest, and with that, me being the lightest, I was the most efficient rider at that point. But then on the other side of the mountain, when it's time to ride down, we chose heavier riders to get the most out of the regenerative current of the battery and recharge the batteries on the way down.

(VO14) TENS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE WATCHED THEIR PROGRESS VIRTUALLY FROM DAILY POSTS.

Instagram: Stephan Lacock
Welcome to Ride Day Four. We are now in Malawi. Moment of the day, without speaking to the locals, they brought a soccer ball and we just started playing and it was awesome to see, not being able to speak to them yet, and we were having a great time, and um quite sweaty now but excited for the rest of the journey.

Erin Bates: Was the bike a good tool for breaking the ice and maybe even overcoming the language barrier?

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
Yes, no, it was a great tool for that…it really touched you that you bring this modern piece of technology into this rural community, and you're expecting to find, you know, suffering and everything you do find that, but at the same time, you're finding a lot of joy and excitement. And that just showed me that people are more ready for product, and the product is considered both are ready for each other, so it's now just bringing that together.

Jason with Children: This has been a really good day of charging the sun here at Chitemba, Zambia…and using: one, two, three, SOLAR!

Ryno Lacock
Electrical Engineer
What I’ve learned with the team is that if one thinks a bit out of the box, there’s a vast amount of potential out there. We would pick a spot, we'll pull off the road, and we'll pack out our panels. And the next moment we charging that piece at 5.3 kilowatts, you know, right over there. So can you imagine if we harvest that potential by rolling out infrastructure in a dispersed manner that can actually utilize that?

ERIN BATES: AFTER SEVENTEEN DAYS ON THE ROAD, THE TEAM FINALLY MADE IT HOME, IN SOMETHING OF A SPRINT FINISH, DRIVING A WHOPPING THOUSAND KMS IN A SINGLE DAY.

Prof Thinus Booysen
Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University
I thought it was utterly reckless, but the team decided against my better judgment, that they want to set a record.

Handré: What’s up! Ready? Let’s go man, let’s go.

Masa Kituyi
Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric
I started riding at 3am in the morning, and it was five degrees, absolutely freezing. I couldn't feel my feet, my hands. I was not enjoying myself for the first 100 kilometers, but by the time that the sun came up and we started getting a bit warmer, we got into the flow of things.

Stephan Lacock Soundup: See you later, we will be chasing the sun, very fast now.

(VO15) ON DAY 16, THE SOLAR TEAM IN THE BOSKRAAI BAKKIE CHASED THE BIKE ALL THE WAY FROM THE KAROO TO CAPE AGULHAS.

Off camera voice Soundup: Can you smell the ocean?
Stephan Lacock Soundup: I can smell the ocean!

Dr Jason Samuels
CEO, GreenX Engineering
It was at 800 kilometers when we caught up and we were filming all of that behind the scenes, basically, of seeing them and of celebrating, it was, it was phenomenal.

(VO16) AND NOW HOME, THE REAL WORK BEGINS.
ENGINEERS IN STELLENBOSCH AND NAIROBI WILL CRUNCH THE DATA FROM THE TRIP.
THIS WILL FEED INTO THE PRACTICAL WORK STUDENTS ARE DOING AT THE UNIVERSITY’S ELECTRICITY MOBILITY LAB.

Prof Thinus Booysen upsound: So this is our baby…

THE NEXT PROJECT IS RETROFITTING A BEETLE FOR AN ELECTRIC TRIP, MAYBE TO NAMIBIA?

Stephan Lacock
PhD student, Stellenbosch University
We can have a great time with electric mobility in South Africa. We just need to start making that mind shift. And I really think this trip, this journey, it inspired me, and will inspire a lot of people, and I hope that that inspiration will take fruit and people will actually start pushing this forward.

(VO17) AN ELECTRIC TAXI AND BUS WERE THE FIRST STEPS OF THIS ELECTRIC MOBILITY JOURNEY. THE EPIC MOTORBIKE ROAD TRIP HAS GIVEN THINUS AND HIS TEAM EVEN GREATER MOMENTUM.

Endsit

PROMO 1

(VO) CHASING THE SUN FOR SIX THOUSAND KILOMETRES..
So we were racing against the clock, getting to know one another…
(VO) A SMALL TEAM OF ENGINEERS RISES TO THE CHALLENGE
It’s one thing to drive an electric motorcycle, but we soon realised that we want to change people's perspective around electric mobility, specifically.

PROMO 2
(VO) FROM DAWN TO DUSK, DEPENDENT ON THE SUN…
We were on such a tight timeline and we had to keep driving and keep doing kilometres, you fear that one cloudy day can ruin the whole thing.
(VO) AN ELECTRIC MOTORBIKE DOES THE DISTANCE IN A STUNT TO SHOW OFF THE SCIENCE

PROMO 3
(VO) SETTING A GOAL AND RACING TO MEET IT
A lot was on the line because everyone is watching us now.
I started riding at 3 am in the morning, it was absolutely freezing.
(VO) PUSHING TECHNOLOGY TO THE VERY LIMITS IN A FINAL SPRINT
I thought it was utterly reckless, but the team decided against my better judgement that they want to set a record

They then set out and drove 6000km through Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia and Botswana to South Africa, experiencing sun, clouds, rain and hail, traffic and empty landscapes. They camped most nights where they stopped, on the side of the road. They travelled as two teams over 17 days. Every morning the solar panel team would set off at about 4:00 am, drive 200km to find a good sunny spot to put down the solar panels – a soccer field, or a river bed, or just by the side of the road. This team would charge the huge battery they had bought from South Africa while waiting for the motor-biker to arrive. At first light, the motorbike would set out with a support car, swapping out the small electric battery every 50 to 100kms, depending on weather and traffic conditions. Once the biker had caught up with the solar panel team, they would do another set of battery swaps and swap the bike-rider out. All this time, the solar panels would be recharging the big mother battery which would also be used to power the bike batteries at night. Then the biker would set out again and do another 200 kms about to find the place where they could camp for the night. And at about four, once the sun started losing its power and angles, the solar panel team would pack up and follow them, getting there at about 08h00 pm to set up camp for the night, and prepare for a 4 am start the next morning. This above information would be best presented or supported by a graphic with a map to show their route. The video diary is fairly shakily shot with moments captured here and there, rather than a cinematographic spread. But there are some splendid drone shots which are very useful and it is more cinema verité than National Geographic. They have 1.2 TBs which is usefully organised and labelled. The students were collecting data on battery consumption and vehicle efficiency, which is to show how many units of energy they used per km to show that EV’s are viable over long-distance, even without charging stations. They discovered that there were a number of factors which impacted on their progress: They weight of the driver The contour and steepness of the road The weather, in particular the wind while driving The weather, in particular when there was not sun enough to power the batteries through the solar panels The traffic – driving behind big trucks protected them from the wind and saved energy The temperature – the higher the better The efficiency of the driving – the more acceleration, the harder on the battery The speed they drove While the quest was a scientific experiment, it also became a personal and emotional journey for the participants. They found that they could break down barriers between people and themselves by explaining the electric bike and interacting with people along the way. There are some good moments that are caught on camera of these interactions, but not beautifully shot. Tension moments on the road were: • When it rained in Malawi and their progress was slowed down due to lack of sun and camping space • When it hailed – more of a surprise than anything else • When they set up the solar panel field next to the Lusaka airport and police tried to chase them away (no visuals of police but visuals of their solar camp) • When they moved away from the equator and the tilt of the earth required a greater tilt of the solar panels to capture the sun’s rays, and they battled to find the right things to prop them up on • A decision to do a 1000km final day finish to show that the motorbike could do that distance in a single day – and then made it. Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 13 January 2025 15 December 2024 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 11 December 2024 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: (VO1) HERE COMES THE SUN…. A SOURCE OF LIGHT…AND POWER…. IT WAS SUNSHINE THAT POWERED THIS ELECTRIC MOTORBIKE OVER SIX THOUSAND KILOMETRES….. ON AN EPIC ROAD TRIP ACROSS AFRICA. Stephan Lacock soundup: We only had 19 days… Jason Samuels soundup: A lot was on the line… Thinus Booysen soundup: We were really scared that it wasn't going to work… Masa Kituyi soundup: Everyone thought that we were crazy when we started saying that we're going to do this trip. ERIN BATES: THE ROAD-TRIP WAS A BOLD IDEA, HATCHED BY ENGINEERS FROM STELLENBOSCH UNIVERSITY WHICH IS PIONEERING RESEARCH ON ELECTRIC TRANSPORT IN AFRICA. (VO2) INITIALLY THE PROJECT WAS AN ATTEMPT TO SOLVE A PROBLEM: HOW TO GET TWO BATTERY-POWERED ELECTRIC MOTOR-BIKES FROM NAIROBI IN KENYA TO THE CAMPUS, AS PART OF A RESEARCH PARTNERSHIP BETWEEN THE UNIVERSITY AND A COMPANY CALLED ROAM ELECTRIC. Stephan Lacock Soundup: Dis gerreid op 200 kilogram… AND IN THIS DIFFICULTY, PROFESSOR THINUS BOOYSEN OF THE ENGINEERING FACULTY SAW AN OPPORTUNITY. Prof Thinus Booysen Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University The quotes for couriers were just too much, or they weren't willing to travel with the batteries….and we said, we have six weeks. Let's plan this. Let's go up into Africa, get the bikes, ride them down, and then make a spectacle out of it. (VO3) THINUS UPPED THE ANTE BY INSISTING ON USING GREEN ENERGY ON A ROUTE THAT HAS NO ELECTRICAL CHARGING STATIONS. SO HE AND HIS PHD STUDENT, STEPHAN LACOCK, STARTED TO IMAGINE HOW THIS MIGHT WORK USING A COMBINATION OF SOLAR PANELS AND BATTERIES. Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University We didn’t know if it was possible, but the more effort we put in the more I realised it’s actually possibly and we just kept on pushing. Prof Thinus Booysen Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University I spent weekends doing and redoing the math, because it's actually quite complicated. You have to think about the dynamics of the vehicle that's carrying the solar panels, and the motorbike, and understand how many kilometres you can do in a day, because they can never go too far away from one another, (VO4) THEY DESIGNED A TRAVELLING POP-UP SOLAR PANEL ARRAY, WHICH THEY BELIEVED COULD GET THE TWO-WHEELER ABOUT 400 KMS A DAY. Sound-Up: Time is of the essence. It is a thing. (VO5) TEN SOLAR PANELS AND A LARGE BATTERY BANK WERE FITTED INTO A CUSTOMISED BAKKIE WHICH THEY CALLED THE BOSKRAAI. Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University I mean, the amount of weight that was in the back of that bakkie was just unbelievable. It was anything close to 1.2 tons. A lot of engineers, a lot of opinions went into one wooden box, but I mean it helped it's durability and everything in structure. Sound-Up: Now for the last final check! (VO6) SOME OF THE TEAM DROVE UP TO NAIROBI. OTHERS JETTED IN, INCLUDING A SOLAR EXPERT, ONE OF THINUS’S FORMER STUDENTS, DR JASON SAMUELS. JASON’S JOB WAS TO CHASE THE SUN IN THE BOSKRAAI BAKKIE AND SET UP THE SOLAR PANELS TO HARVEST MAXIMUM POWER. Dr Jason Samuels CEO, GreenX Engineering We'd have to find a perfect spot ….. somewhere where it's open, but we could still get some community interaction, somewhere we not have a lot of shading, and also somewhere we will where we would not be chased away. (VO7) BUT FIRST, THE SOUTH AFRICANS MET A KEY MEMBER OF THE TEAM, KENYAN MASA KITUYI, A VETERAN MOTOR-CROSS RACER. AS AN ENGINEER, MASA HAD PLAYED A KEY ROLE IN DEVELOPING THE BIKE THEY WERE TAKING TO STELLENBOSCH. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric For me, it was always on the bucket list. I've always wanted to drive, uh, ride a motorcycle across Africa, but it was a bit daunting to do it on a motorbike that you've developed and been building for quite a while. (VO8) THE ROAM-AIR MOTORBIKE IS RUGGED AND POPULAR ON THE STREETS OF NAIROBI. - THE FACTORY PRODUCES 40 BIKES A DAY, AND IS POISED TO CAPITALISE ON THE GROWING DEMAND FOR ELECTRIC VEHICLES. Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University When you walk through the door, there's this massive warehouse, and it's just electric motorcycles everywhere. (VO9) EACH BIKE CARRIES TWO BATTERIES WHICH CAN BE CHARGED FROM A DOMESTIC POWER PLUG AND SWAPPED OUT. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric The motor bikes are used as a workhorse by Boda Boda riders around town, and they ride 13 hours a day, every single day. We've designed it to carry up to 220 kilos of payload. (VO10) NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME THE BIKE WAS GOING TO BE TESTED ON DISTANCE - A 6000 KM ROUTE WHICH TRAVERSED SIX AFRICAN COUNTRIES. ON THE 29TH OF SEPTEMBER THE TEAM SET OFF, KNOWING THAT THEY HAD TO QUICKLY SET UP A BATTERY-POWERING AND SWAPPING ROUTINE. Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University Every morning, around 4:30am I woke up, along with the team, we looked at the weather apps, with four weather apps just checking: where's the sun going to shine? (VO11) THE DRIVING TEAM SET OFF AN HOUR AFTER THE SOLAR TEAM, WITH A BACK UP VEHICLE BEHIND, OFTEN DRIVEN BY STEFAN’S FATHER, RYNO LACOCK. RYNO HAS SPENT DECADES MANAGING ESKOM POWER PLANTS - NOW HE WAS CHAPERONING THE NEXT GENERATION AND LETTING THEM TAKE THE LEAD. Ryno Lacock Electrical Engineer I ended up being the old cliche, chief cook and bottle washer on the trip because I was facilitating the whole thing in terms of camping and the cooking and so on Ryno Lacock Upsound: Alright Masa we have calculated our distance to the solar team and what they are receiving, so you have a green light. …You have done 87.2 kilometeres already, 87.2. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric It did feel very clean as we moved around, just harnessing the sun's energy, but it did add quite a lot of pressure onto the timeline. Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University The motorcycle really had to go through quite different environments in terms of altitude, plateaus, you know, temperature, rain, everything. (VO12) PROGRESS HINGED ON A CLEAR SKY. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric We need to make sure that we have sunlight and that that did change the dynamic a lot. You can plan as much as you want, but Mother Nature has its own say in what to do. Instagram: Stephan Lacock We are here in a hail storm in the middle of Maka Bako in Tanzania, crazy to see the people’s reactions, our own as well, slipping a lot, but very cool and excited. Masa Kituyi soundup: It’s been a crazy afternoon. I am happy I am still warm and dry! (VO13) THE TEAM HAD TO WORK WITH THEIR OWN BODY WEIGHT FOR MAXIMUM EFFICIENCY. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric In Malawi, we were driving up 2000 meters above sea level, climb from the Lake Malawi up into the forest, and with that, me being the lightest, I was the most efficient rider at that point. But then on the other side of the mountain, when it's time to ride down, we chose heavier riders to get the most out of the regenerative current of the battery and recharge the batteries on the way down. (VO14) TENS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE WATCHED THEIR PROGRESS VIRTUALLY FROM DAILY POSTS. Instagram: Stephan Lacock Welcome to Ride Day Four. We are now in Malawi. Moment of the day, without speaking to the locals, they brought a soccer ball and we just started playing and it was awesome to see, not being able to speak to them yet, and we were having a great time, and um quite sweaty now but excited for the rest of the journey. Erin Bates: Was the bike a good tool for breaking the ice and maybe even overcoming the language barrier? Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University Yes, no, it was a great tool for that…it really touched you that you bring this modern piece of technology into this rural community, and you're expecting to find, you know, suffering and everything you do find that, but at the same time, you're finding a lot of joy and excitement. And that just showed me that people are more ready for product, and the product is considered both are ready for each other, so it's now just bringing that together. Jason with Children: This has been a really good day of charging the sun here at Chitemba, Zambia…and using: one, two, three, SOLAR! Ryno Lacock Electrical Engineer What I’ve learned with the team is that if one thinks a bit out of the box, there’s a vast amount of potential out there. We would pick a spot, we'll pull off the road, and we'll pack out our panels. And the next moment we charging that piece at 5.3 kilowatts, you know, right over there. So can you imagine if we harvest that potential by rolling out infrastructure in a dispersed manner that can actually utilize that? ERIN BATES: AFTER SEVENTEEN DAYS ON THE ROAD, THE TEAM FINALLY MADE IT HOME, IN SOMETHING OF A SPRINT FINISH, DRIVING A WHOPPING THOUSAND KMS IN A SINGLE DAY. Prof Thinus Booysen Faculty of Engineering, Stellenbosch University I thought it was utterly reckless, but the team decided against my better judgment, that they want to set a record. Handré: What’s up! Ready? Let’s go man, let’s go. Masa Kituyi Roam Air Product Owner, Roam Electric I started riding at 3am in the morning, and it was five degrees, absolutely freezing. I couldn't feel my feet, my hands. I was not enjoying myself for the first 100 kilometers, but by the time that the sun came up and we started getting a bit warmer, we got into the flow of things. Stephan Lacock Soundup: See you later, we will be chasing the sun, very fast now. (VO15) ON DAY 16, THE SOLAR TEAM IN THE BOSKRAAI BAKKIE CHASED THE BIKE ALL THE WAY FROM THE KAROO TO CAPE AGULHAS. Off camera voice Soundup: Can you smell the ocean? Stephan Lacock Soundup: I can smell the ocean! Dr Jason Samuels CEO, GreenX Engineering It was at 800 kilometers when we caught up and we were filming all of that behind the scenes, basically, of seeing them and of celebrating, it was, it was phenomenal. (VO16) AND NOW HOME, THE REAL WORK BEGINS. ENGINEERS IN STELLENBOSCH AND NAIROBI WILL CRUNCH THE DATA FROM THE TRIP. THIS WILL FEED INTO THE PRACTICAL WORK STUDENTS ARE DOING AT THE UNIVERSITY’S ELECTRICITY MOBILITY LAB. Prof Thinus Booysen upsound: So this is our baby… THE NEXT PROJECT IS RETROFITTING A BEETLE FOR AN ELECTRIC TRIP, MAYBE TO NAMIBIA? Stephan Lacock PhD student, Stellenbosch University We can have a great time with electric mobility in South Africa. We just need to start making that mind shift. And I really think this trip, this journey, it inspired me, and will inspire a lot of people, and I hope that that inspiration will take fruit and people will actually start pushing this forward. (VO17) AN ELECTRIC TAXI AND BUS WERE THE FIRST STEPS OF THIS ELECTRIC MOBILITY JOURNEY. THE EPIC MOTORBIKE ROAD TRIP HAS GIVEN THINUS AND HIS TEAM EVEN GREATER MOMENTUM. Endsit PROMO 1 (VO) CHASING THE SUN FOR SIX THOUSAND KILOMETRES.. So we were racing against the clock, getting to know one another… (VO) A SMALL TEAM OF ENGINEERS RISES TO THE CHALLENGE It’s one thing to drive an electric motorcycle, but we soon realised that we want to change people's perspective around electric mobility, specifically. PROMO 2 (VO) FROM DAWN TO DUSK, DEPENDENT ON THE SUN… We were on such a tight timeline and we had to keep driving and keep doing kilometres, you fear that one cloudy day can ruin the whole thing. (VO) AN ELECTRIC MOTORBIKE DOES THE DISTANCE IN A STUNT TO SHOW OFF THE SCIENCE PROMO 3 (VO) SETTING A GOAL AND RACING TO MEET IT A lot was on the line because everyone is watching us now. I started riding at 3 am in the morning, it was absolutely freezing. (VO) PUSHING TECHNOLOGY TO THE VERY LIMITS IN A FINAL SPRINT I thought it was utterly reckless, but the team decided against my better judgement that they want to set a record

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight we let the sun power us across Africa on a rugged motorbike with a team of scientists...proving it can be done
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We will tell a story of a group of students and academics who proved that the African sun can power a locally-made motorbike across four countries from Nairobi to Stellenbosch in two and a half weeks, despite there being no charging stations on the route. While being a scientific experiment, it was also a stunt to raise awareness about the potential for Electric Vehicles in Africa, while championing local skills, both the expertise of the students from the US and in the ROAM motorbike factory in Kenya.
metadata.Summary: The story will be told through interviews with the four people below, a bit of B-Roll filmed in their interviews, and through a daily video diary the team kept as they travelled 17 days from Nairobi and Stellenbosch, arriving here on the 16th of October. It was the brainchild of PROF THINUS BOOYSEN, founder of the University of Stellenbosch’s Electric Mobility Lab, who is pushing research in affordable electric vehicles that are rugged enough for the African continent, for working people, and made on the continent. The motorbikes were mostly driven by Stellenbosch Doctoral Student STEPHAN LACOCK and Kenyan engineer MASALULE KITUYI of ROAM, the Swedish-Kenyan company that makes these tough, rugged Electrical motorbikes. In Kenya, they are used a lot as delivery bikes. Tther members of the team, which included Stephan’s father and brother, and THINUS BOOYSEN, also drove the bike as part of the team experience. We also interview DR JASON SAMUELS who works in a private company GREENX across the road from the Department of Electrical Engineering, and was in charge of the solar panel element of the trip. His company puts up solar panels on schools across the country, sponsored by the University of Stellenbosch. His dream is to use this research to build a model where schools can power their electric buses with the solar power on the roofs to provide transport locally for school kids. When we do the interview, he will take us to a school and show us what he does. It will provide us with a different but clear application of renewable energy visually. The three South African interviews are confirmed, but I am still waiting to hear if we can interview MASA KITUYI by zoom as he is back in Nairobi. MASA KITUYI is the lead engineer on the ROAM motorbike product, and a motorbike stunt driver.
